record.paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
record.context_brief: Morphological set representations and invariant losses
record.original_question: Are compact morphological representations of sets, such as skeleton-based representations, extrema of signed distance functions, and shape-size distributions from granulometries, more efficient for handling permutation invariance in machine-learning tasks on sets or graphs, and can loss functions based on such morphological descriptions be made inherently permutation-invariant and scale-invariant?

evidence.quote: Are morphological compact representations of sets more efficient to deal with permutation invariance in machine learning? Can we introduce loss functions based on morphological descriptions which are inherently permutation-invariant and scale-invariant?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote a class of compact subsets (or finite point sets, or graphs viewed via their vertex sets in some embedding) of $\mathbb{R}^d$. For $X \in \mathcal{S}$, consider the following morphological descriptors:

(i) The skeleton $\mathrm{Sk}(X)$, defined as the set of centers of maximal inscribed balls of $X$, together with the radius function on $\mathrm{Sk}(X)$.

(ii) The signed distance function $d_X : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, with $d_X(z) = \mathrm{dist}(z, \partial X)$ for $z \in X$ and $d_X(z) = -\mathrm{dist}(z, \partial X)$ for $z \notin X$, together with its local extrema.

(iii) The granulometric (shape–size) distribution $G_X(r) = \mu(X \setminus (X \circ B_r))$, where $B_r$ is the closed Euclidean ball of radius $r$, $\circ$ is morphological opening, and $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure.

These descriptors are by construction invariant under permutations of any underlying point-cloud parametrization of $X$.

Address the following:

(a) Construct an encoder $\Phi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ built from descriptors (i)–(iii) (or combinations thereof) and prove that, on a specified class of inputs, $\Phi$ is more "efficient" than standard permutation-invariant set encoders (e.g. Deep Sets-type aggregators) in a precise quantitative sense — for instance, achieving universal approximation of continuous permutation-invariant functions on $\mathcal{S}$ with strictly smaller embedding dimension $k$ or with provably lower sample complexity for a chosen learning task.

(b) Exhibit a loss function $L(X, Y)$ on $\mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{S}$, defined purely in terms of the morphological descriptors above, that satisfies simultaneously:
 - permutation invariance: $L(X, Y) = L(\sigma(X), \tau(Y))$ for any reorderings $\sigma, \tau$ of any chosen parametrization;
 - scale invariance: $L(\lambda X, \lambda Y) = L(X, Y)$ for all $\lambda > 0$;
 - the metric (or at least pseudometric) axioms on the quotient of $\mathcal{S}$ by the group generated by permutations and positive scalings.

Either provide such an encoder and loss with proofs of the stated properties and efficiency gains, or prove that no such construction can outperform existing permutation-invariant set representations in the prescribed sense.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning whether morphological compact representations of sets yield more efficient permutation-invariant and scale-invariant learning architectures and losses. No definitive resolution appears in the literature; related work on permutation-invariant set encoders (Deep Sets) and on morphological neural networks exists, but a precise affirmative or negative answer to this question has not been established.
